title: Cordoba, city of lights
hookLine: a great city with lit streets, baths and libraries

lines: A CITY RULED BY ANOTHER FAITH.
cards: In a convent in Saxony, far to the north, a nun named Hrotsvitha sits down to write a poem. She is a Christian, writing in Latin, about a Christian boy named Pelagius who died in a Muslim city.
And when she names that city, she praises it. She calls it the ornament of the world: a city far from her convent, ruled by people of another faith.
The city is Cordoba, on the river Guadalquivir, in the heart of al-Andalus.

teach.b: What made a faraway nun reach for that phrase?

Later Arabic writers, whose accounts al-Maqqari gathered in his history of al-Andalus, describe a city of markets and gardens, public baths, water brought in for drinking and washing, libraries, and streets where you could walk at night by the light of lamps.
That's the picture behind the name city of lights. Hold it a little carefully.
Some of those descriptions were written long after, by people who missed Cordoba, and longing polishes a memory. But the outline holds: this was a capital of books, scholars and craftsmen.
And it was a city of more than one faith.
Muslims, Christians and Jews lived in its streets, not always in peace, and not always as equals, but close enough to share a language.
A Christian writer of Cordoba named Paul Alvarus complained that the young men of his church were so taken with Arabic poetry and Arabic books that they neglected their own Latin.
His complaint shows how strong the pull of Arabic culture was, even on those who worried about it. Hrotsvitha's poem holds both sides too.
It praises the city, and it's harsh about the ruler at whose order the boy was killed.
A golden city, and a real one, with light and shadow.
So when you hear the ornament of the world, hear it in a Christian nun's voice, from far away, giving a city of another faith that word.

how: Cordoba is remembered in Muslim histories as a center of Islamic learning in al-Andalus, and visitors today walk its old streets and its great mosque.

o: a fortress town where Tariq's army first landed in Spain
a North African city that ruled over Spain's coast
the capital of al-Andalus, praised as the world's ornament

games.q: you're a Christian writer in Cordoba. the young men of your church read Arabic poetry and Arabic books with delight. what do you do?
o: learn Arabic yourself and join them.
write a complaint that they're neglecting Latin.
say nothing; it's none of your business.
games.why: Paul Alvarus wrote a complaint: they knew Arabic eloquence and neglected their own Latin. his worry shows how strong the pull of the city's Arabic culture was.

practice: See a river, dark and slow, a bridge over it, and streets beyond with small pools of lamplight: a bath house with steam in the doorway, someone closing a bookshop, a call to prayer from one direction, a church bell from another, a family lighting candles in a third house.
Then let the old city fade and see your own street at night, with its own lights and its own people. If you pray, you can hold them all; if not, just let them be there in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Cordoba. The capital of al-Andalus on the Guadalquivir, a city of lamps, baths and books that a Saxon nun called the ornament of the world. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Qurtuba, the Arabic name for Cordoba.

carryVoice: Your line: the ornament of the world. Light and shadow, and both of them real. Until tomorrow.
